def: Training a model from scratch on a very large text corpus to predict the next token, which gives it general language knowledge before any adaptation.
The weights saying what fraction of training tokens come from each source (web, code, books and so on); small valuable sources are often seen several times.
Removing exact and near-duplicate documents from training data, often with MinHash and Jaccard similarity, to save compute and reduce memorisation.
A fitted power-law relationship that predicts loss from parameters, tokens or compute, used to plan training runs before spending the compute.
Choosing parameters $N$ and tokens $D$ to minimise loss for a fixed compute budget $C \approx 6ND$; the Chinchilla result is roughly 20 tokens per parameter.
Computing in 16-bit formats such as BF16 while keeping FP32 master weights and optimizer states, which saves memory and time without losing small updates.
Splitting optimizer states (stage 1), gradients (stage 2) and parameters (stage 3) across data-parallel GPUs so each stores only its share; FSDP is the PyTorch counterpart.
Storing only some activations and recomputing the rest during the backward pass, trading about 33% more compute for a large cut in activation memory.
Splitting one model's computation across GPUs, either inside each layer (tensor parallelism) or by groups of layers (pipeline parallelism).
How the learning rate changes during training; the usual choice is a linear warmup to a peak followed by a cosine decay to a small floor.
Training a pretrained model on prompt-response pairs with next-token loss on the response, which teaches it to follow instructions in a chat format.
Excluding prompt tokens from the loss during SFT so that only the response tokens, including the end-of-turn token, produce gradients.
A network that scores a response with one scalar, trained on preference pairs with the Bradley-Terry loss $-\log\sigma(r_w - r_l)$.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: optimising a policy against a learned reward model while a KL penalty keeps it close to a reference model.
A loss that trains directly on chosen and rejected pairs, $-\log\sigma(\beta[\Delta_w - \Delta_l])$, equivalent to the KL-regularised RLHF objective without a reward model or RL loop.
Low-rank adaptation: freeze a weight matrix $W_0$ and learn $\Delta W = \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$, adding only $r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})$ trainable parameters per matrix.
LoRA on top of a frozen base quantised to 4-bit NF4 with double-quantised block scales, about 4.127 bits per weight, so large models fine-tune on small GPUs.
Training a small student to match a larger teacher's temperature-softened output distribution with a $T^2$-scaled KL loss, or to imitate text the teacher generated.
The first layer of a vision transformer: each $P \times P$ image patch is flattened and linearly projected into a token, giving $HW/P^2$ tokens per image.
The CLIP-style loss that pulls matching image-text pairs together and pushes mismatched pairs apart, as cross-entropy over the rows and columns of a similarity matrix.
